946.title: Have you seen God?
946.hook: a skeptical student asks every teacher the same question, and one says yes
946.carry: the rishis saw, and so can you
946.howItsDone: Vivekananda's Raja Yoga is read and studied in Ramakrishna Mission and Vedanta Society centers, often alongside Patanjali's Yoga Sutras, and students describe starting with posture, breath and watching the mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a week of work ended with Karma Yoga's ideal: the silence of the desert in the middle of the busiest street.
screen: `KARMA YOGA.` · `A DESERT IN THE BUSY STREET.`

segments.voice: Calcutta, in the early 1880s. A college student named Narendranath Datta is sharp, restless and hard to impress. He goes from one religious teacher to another with a single blunt question: have you seen God? He gets speeches, and arguments, and no straight answer. Then he meets a temple priest at Dakshineswar, Ramakrishna, and asks him too. And Ramakrishna, by Narendra's own later account, says yes: he sees God the way he sees the young man in front of him, only more intensely. And, the early biographies add, he offers to show Narendra too. That student became Swami Vivekananda.
screen: `ONE QUESTION: HAVE YOU SEEN GOD?` → `SPEECHES, NO ANSWER.` → `RAMAKRISHNA: YES.`

segments.voice: Years later, Vivekananda built a whole book on that answer. It's called Raja Yoga, the yoga of the mind, and it opens with an argument. The great teachers of religion, he says, did not only believe. They saw. They spoke of what they had perceived for themselves. That's an old Hindu idea, not a new one. The poets of the Vedas are called rishis, seers, and tradition says the Vedas weren't made up by them but seen and heard. So, Vivekananda says, if one person has perceived something, others can perceive it too, given the right method. Religion, in his telling, shouldn't rest only on someone else's report. It can be tested by experience. And Raja Yoga asks for no belief at the start. Try it, and see. Then the twist. The lab isn't somewhere else. The instrument is the mind itself, and it doesn't hold still long enough to observe anything. So the book gets practical: posture, breath, learning to watch the mind. Its second half carries his rendering of Patanjali's Yoga Sutras, which open: now, the teaching of yoga. This is why many Hindu teachers speak of faith less as a list of opinions to sign and more as practice: the sit, the name, the prayer, done until you see for yourself. So when someone asks, do you really believe all that, a Hindu can honestly say: my tradition invites me to look.
screen: `THE TEACHERS DIDN'T ONLY BELIEVE; THEY SAW.` · `THE RISHIS ARE SEERS.` · `TEST IT BY EXPERIENCE.` · `THE LAB IS THE MIND ITSELF.`

segments.voice: Treat this sit as a first experiment: back upright but easy, the breath at its own pace, nothing to reach. Every few breaths, ask quietly what your mind is doing right now, planning, remembering, listening, drifting, answer honestly with one word, and go back to the breath. If you pray, you can begin or end with a prayer you already know.
Raja Yoga. Vivekananda's book on the yoga of the mind, which asks you to try, and see, before you believe.
Your line: the rishis saw, and so can you. Tomorrow, the experiment meets a monkey. That's day nine hundred forty-six.

947.title: The drunken monkey
947.hook: a monkey, some wine, a scorpion, and the one watching the mind
947.carry: you are the watcher, not the monkey
947.howItsDone: Students of Vivekananda's Raja Yoga often begin with short daily sits in which they let the mind wander and simply observe it, before moving on to concentration practices; the book is read and studied in Ramakrishna Mission and Vedanta Society centers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Narendra asked Ramakrishna, have you seen God?, and Raja Yoga made the mind the lab. Your line: the rishis saw, and so can you.

Start with a monkey. Restless already, the way monkeys are, never on one branch for long. Now somebody gives it wine to drink, and it gets wilder. Then a scorpion stings it, and it leaps about in pain. And then, as if that weren't enough, a demon gets inside it. That's the creature Vivekananda asks his readers to look at in Raja Yoga. He isn't talking about animals. He's describing the thing doing the reading.
screen: `A RESTLESS MONKEY.` → `WINE, A SCORPION, A DEMON.` → `HE MEANS THE MIND.`

segments.voice: The picture comes in his chapter on pratyahara and dharana, drawing the mind in and holding it steady. He takes it piece by piece. The mind is restless by nature, like the monkey. Then desire gets into it: that is the wine. Jealousy at someone else's good fortune stings it: the scorpion. Last comes pride, the demon, and now it thinks nothing in the world matters but itself. You might expect a scolding next. Instead comes a gentle first lesson. Sit for a while, he says, and let the mind run on. Don't fight it. Just watch it. Some of the thoughts, he warns, may astonish you. Keep watching anyway. With practice, he says, the jumping slowly lessens. Underneath that advice sits one of the big ideas of Hindu yoga. In the Yoga Sutras, the mind belongs to what is seen, part of nature, prakriti. You, the one who sees, are something else: the purusha, the seer. Vedanta has its own word for it, the sakshi, the witness. So the monkey is real, but it isn't you. That's why watching comes first. Until the watching starts, the mind simply is the monkey, swinging from a worry to a text message to an old argument, and calling it thinking. The moment a jump is noticed, there's a little gap. The one watching and the jump are not the same thing. That gap is where Raja Yoga begins.
screen: `THE MONKEY IS RESTLESS BY NATURE.` · `WINE, SCORPION, DEMON: DESIRE, JEALOUSY, PRIDE.` · `FIRST LESSON: LET IT RUN, AND WATCH.` · then, large: `THE SEER IS NOT THE MONKEY.`

segments.voice: Try the first lesson exactly as it's given: don't try to calm anything, let the mind run, and when a thought jumps up, a plan, a memory, a complaint, just notice it, the way you'd watch a monkey move between branches from a park bench. No chasing it, no shooing it away, and if a thought comes that you'd rather not have, let it be seen too. If you pray, you can hold the watching itself as your prayer.
Raja Yoga. Vivekananda's yoga of the mind, which begins by watching the mind jump, from the seat of the one who sees.
Your line: you are the watcher, not the monkey. Tomorrow, another of his pictures: a lake, and what lives at the bottom of it. Day nine hundred forty-seven, and counting.

948.title: The lake and the self
948.hook: you can't see the bottom of a lake while the wind is blowing
948.carry: still the waves, and the self shows
948.howItsDone: People who follow Vivekananda's teaching read Patanjali's Yoga Sutras with his explanations and keep a daily sit aimed at quieting the mind; the Ramakrishna Mission and Vedanta Societies hold classes on the text.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raja Yoga's monkey: restless, drunk on desire, stung by jealousy, possessed by pride. Your line: you are the watcher, not the monkey.

Stand at the edge of a lake on a windy afternoon. The surface is all chop and glitter. Somewhere down there are stones, weeds, maybe a lost key, but you can't see any of it. Come back at dawn, when the air is still. The same water. Now you can count the pebbles. Nothing was added to the lake overnight. Something was taken away. Vivekananda uses that lake to explain one short line near the start of the Yoga Sutras.
screen: `A LAKE ON A WINDY DAY.` → `THE SAME LAKE AT DAWN.` → `NOTHING ADDED. SOMETHING STILLED.`

segments.voice: Raja Yoga carries, in its second half, Vivekananda's rendering of the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali, short lines with his explanation under each. Near the very start is the line that says what yoga is. Put plainly: yoga is the stilling of the waves of the mind. The Sanskrit word for the mind-stuff is chitta. The word for its waves is vritti. And Vivekananda reaches for a lake. The bottom of the lake, he says, is our own true self. The lake is the chitta, and the waves are the vrittis. While the surface is rippled, or the water muddy, we can't see the bottom. Only when the water is clear and the waves die down do we see what was there the whole time. In the Hindu words this path has met, that bottom is the atman, the true self. That changes the goal. Nobody has to build a self, or earn one. In this picture it's already there, and the work is to let the surface settle. This is what yoga means in its home tradition. Posture matters, but in Patanjali it's one step, a steady seat for the mind's work. The stretch class is a doorway. The goal is the still lake. Vivekananda doesn't pretend it's quick. The waves keep rising: a craving, an insult remembered, a plan for tomorrow. Each time one settles, the water is a little clearer.
screen: `YOGA STILLS THE WAVES OF THE MIND.` · `THE LAKE IS CHITTA. THE WAVES ARE VRITTIS.` · `THE BOTTOM IS THE ATMAN, THE TRUE SELF.` · then, large: `NOTHING ADDED. SOMETHING STILLED.`

segments.voice: Picture a lake, any lake, under a little wind, and each time a thought rises, see it as a wave on that surface. Don't push the wave flat; let it be a wave and watch it pass back into the water, big ones and small ones, and between them, for a moment, the surface may go still. If you pray, you can rest in that stillness as your prayer.
Raja Yoga. Vivekananda's yoga of the mind, which he explains with a lake: still the waves, and the bottom, the true self, was there all along.
Your line: still the waves, and the self shows. Nothing is added to the lake, only something stilled. See you tomorrow.

949.title: Who am I?
949.hook: a sixteen-year-old lies down as if dead and asks what's left
949.carry: i am not the body or the mind
949.howItsDone: People who follow Ramana's teaching practice self-inquiry, turning attention back to the sense of 'I' and asking 'who am I?'; Who Am I? is read and recited at his ashram at the foot of Arunachala in Tiruvannamalai and by readers around the world.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vivekananda's lake: still the waves, and the bottom shows. Your line: still the waves, and the self shows.

Madurai, south India, 1896. A sixteen-year-old schoolboy named Venkataraman is alone in his uncle's house when a sudden fear of death comes over him. He isn't ill. Instead of calling for help, he lies down, stretches out stiff the way a body lies, holds his breath, and asks himself: this body is dead. They'll carry it off and burn it. But am I dead? And he finds, by his own later account, that something is still here, aware, untouched. A few weeks later he leaves home for a holy hill called Arunachala, and stays there for the rest of his life. The world knows him as Ramana Maharshi.
screen: `SIXTEEN, AND AFRAID OF DEATH.` → `HE LIES DOWN AS IF DEAD.` → `BUT AM I DEAD?`

segments.voice: Years later at Arunachala, when tradition says he hardly spoke, a visitor brought him questions, and the answers came back written down. They became a little text called Who Am I? It starts where everyone can check: every being wants to be happy and not to suffer. Happiness, Ramana says, is our real nature, and to find it we need to know ourselves. The way to know yourself is to ask: who am I? The answer moves by taking things away. The body is not I. The senses are not I. The breath is not I. Even the mind, the thing that thinks, is not I. If I am none of these, what am I? What's left, the text says, is awareness, and that is what I am. This is one of Hinduism's biggest teachings, the atman: your true self is not the body and not the mind. The Upanishads walk this road, setting things aside as not this, not this, and Ramana walked it first, on his uncle's floor. Listen to ordinary speech: my hand, my thoughts, my mood. Someone is doing the owning, and Ramana's question is aimed at that owner. So when a bad grade, a mirror or a rough mood tries to tell you who you are, this teaching says: that is something you notice, not what you are. He doesn't ask you to believe it. He asks you to look.
screen: `EVERYONE WANTS TO BE HAPPY.` · `NOT THE BODY, NOT THE SENSES, NOT THE MIND.` · `WHAT REMAINS IS AWARENESS: THE ATMAN.` · then, large: `WHO AM I?`

segments.voice: Notice the body's weight on the seat, then a sound in the room, then a thought passing, and say quietly to each: this is noticed. Now turn gently toward whatever is doing the noticing and ask once, without hurry, who am I, resting your attention there without reaching for words, the way you'd rest your eyes on a far horizon. If you pray, you can let that resting be your prayer.
Ramana Maharshi. The teacher of Arunachala who, at sixteen, asked: am I dead? His little text Who Am I? sets down body, senses and mind, and asks what's left.
Your line: i am not the body or the mind. Tomorrow, how to ask it when the thoughts won't stop. Day nine hundred forty-nine.

950.title: The stick in the fire
950.hook: a stick that tends a fire until the fire takes the stick
950.carry: every thought hangs on the thought 'i'
950.howItsDone: In self-inquiry as Ramana taught it, people meet each passing thought with 'to whom did this come?' and turn back toward the sense of 'I', in sitting practice and through the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramana Maharshi lay down at sixteen and asked who am I. Your line: i am not the body or the mind.

At a cremation fire, someone tends the flames with a long stick, pushing the wood in, turning it so it burns through. It's a plain, sober job. And at the end, when everything has burned, the stick goes into the fire too. Ramana Maharshi takes that stick and puts it in the middle of Who Am I? It's his answer to a question the text raises plainly: what do you do with all these thoughts?
screen: `A STICK TENDS THE FIRE.` → `AT THE END, THE STICK BURNS TOO.` → `WHAT ABOUT ALL THESE THOUGHTS?`

segments.voice: His advice is short. When a thought comes up, don't follow it, and don't argue with it. Instead ask: to whom did this thought come? The answer arrives on its own: to me. Then ask: and who am I? That turns the mind back toward where it came from, he says, and the thought fades. Do it again with the next one. Here's why it works, in his account. All the other thoughts hang on one thought: the thought I. Hindu teachers have an old name for that I-maker: ahankara, the ego. Worries, plans, memories, all of them belong to someone. Follow the I back toward its source, and the rest has nothing to hang on. This is atma-vichara, inquiry into the self, Ramana's whole method. So the question does the job of the stick, turning the other thoughts into the fire. And at the end, Ramana says, it burns up too. Even the question doesn't stay. There's a second picture. Somebody asks whether a seeker first needs to study all the tattvas, the categories philosophers say make up the world and the person. Ramana says no. If you want to throw out the garbage, you don't need to analyze it first. In his account, you don't have to map everything you are not before you ask who you are. You only have to ask.
screen: `TO WHOM DID THIS THOUGHT COME? TO ME.` · `EVERY THOUGHT HANGS ON THE THOUGHT 'I'.` · `THE STICK BURNS AT THE END TOO.` · then, large: `AHANKARA: THE I-MAKER.`

segments.voice: Wait for the first thought, which won't take long, and instead of following its story, ask quietly: to whom did this come? Let the answer be there, to me, then ask who am I, and let the attention turn back toward the one asking, resting there until the next thought arrives, and then again. If you pray, you can let this turning home be your prayer.
Ramana Maharshi. The teacher who said: when a thought comes, ask to whom it came, then ask who am I, and let the question burn up like the stick in the fire.

951.title: The elephant's chain
951.hook: a restless elephant, a chain, and the helps Ramana allows
951.carry: a name of God steadies the reaching mind
951.howItsDone: Some who follow Ramana combine self-inquiry with chanting a divine name, meditating on a form of God, or watching the breath, using these to steady the mind before or alongside asking 'who am I?'.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramana Maharshi's stick at the fire. Your line: every thought hangs on the thought 'i'. Ask to whom it came, then ask who am I.

An elephant walking down a street swings its trunk from side to side. It grabs at a banana stall, a branch, the edge of someone's cart. Nothing malicious. A trunk just reaches. Now give that elephant a chain to hold in its trunk. It carries the chain, and the reaching stops. Ramana Maharshi uses that picture in Who Am I?, in the middle of a plain, practical answer about how to steady a mind that won't settle.
screen: `A TRUNK THAT GRABS AT EVERYTHING.` → `GIVE IT A CHAIN TO HOLD.` → `RAMANA WAS PRACTICAL.`

segments.voice: The question who am I? is the main road in the text. But when Ramana is asked about other practices, he doesn't wave them away. He gives each one a place. First, the breath. The mind and the breath, he says, come from the same source, so when the breath is controlled, the mind quiets too. But the quiet lasts only as long as the breath is held still. When the breath moves again, the mind goes back to its wandering. Breath control is a help, not the destination. Then japa, repeating a name of God, or resting the attention on a form of God. Here's where the elephant comes in. The mind, like that trunk, keeps reaching for one thing after another. Give it one thing to hold, a name, a form, and it steadies. A mind held on one thing, Ramana says, finds the inquiry easier. This is one of the most widely kept Hindu practices. Many Hindus carry a mala, a string of a hundred and eight beads, and say a name on each one: Ram, Krishna, Om Namah Shivaya. So Ramana isn't telling anyone their practice is wrong. The grandmother with her beads, the person who watches the breath, the person who asks who am I: each gets a place, with a plain note on what each one does.
screen: `THE MAIN ROAD: WHO AM I?` · `BREATH AND MIND SHARE ONE SOURCE.` · `JAPA: A NAME OF GOD STEADIES THE MIND.` · then, large: `GIVE THE TRUNK A CHAIN.`

segments.voice: First give the trunk a chain: the breath going in and out at the nose, or, if you pray, a name of God from your own practice, repeated quietly, bringing the attention back each time it reaches for something else. When the mind feels a little steadier, let the chain go and ask once, softly: who am I? Rest wherever that question leaves you.
Ramana Maharshi. The teacher of who am I?, who also made room for the breath and japa, the name of God, as ways to steady a reaching mind.
Your line: a name of God steadies the reaching mind. Tomorrow, the last of these four days: where Ramana says happiness lives. See you there.

952.title: Stay in the shade
952.hook: out of the sun, into the shade, and back out again
952.carry: joy is the self's own, not the thing's
952.howItsDone: Readers of Who Am I? return to it as a daily text; at Ramana's ashram in Tiruvannamalai, visitors sit in silence in the hall where he lived and walk around the hill of Arunachala.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramana Maharshi's elephant. Your line: a name of God steadies the reaching mind.

Midday, a hot road, no wind. A traveler steps under a tree and the relief is instant. A few minutes later, something across the road catches the eye, and the traveler walks back out into the glare to get it. Then back to the shade. Then out again. Ramana Maharshi draws that scene in Who Am I?, near the end, and he uses it to answer the question the text opened with: where is happiness?
screen: `A HOT ROAD AT MIDDAY.` → `INTO THE SHADE, AND OUT AGAIN.` → `WHERE IS HAPPINESS?`

segments.voice: Remember how the text began: everyone wants to be happy. Here, Ramana says where that happiness is. Not in things. When we get something we wanted, we feel happy, and we credit the thing. But what really happened, in his account, is that the wanting stopped for a moment. The mind went quiet and turned back toward the self, and the happiness we felt was the self's own. Vedanta's name for the self is sat-chit-ananda: being, awareness, bliss. Ramana's shade is that ananda. Then the next want shows up, and we walk back into the sun. The one who knows this, he says, stays in the shade. Close by, a line for anyone who feels too far gone. Even someone who has done great wrong, Ramana says, shouldn't sit weeping, I'm a sinner, how can I be saved? Drop that thought, he says, and get on with the inquiry. The heavy story about yourself is one more thought. Now look back at this week. Narendra asking, have you seen God? A monkey, and the one watching it. A lake, and the atman at the bottom. A boy lying down as if dead. The stick that burns at the end. An elephant given a chain. And the shade. Two teachers, and in both their accounts one claim underneath: what the seeker is looking for was there before the looking started.
screen: `HAPPINESS IS NOT IN THINGS.` · `ANANDA: THE SELF'S OWN JOY.` · `DROP THE THOUGHT 'I'M A SINNER.'` · then, large: `THE WISE ONE STAYS IN THE SHADE.`

segments.voice: Recall one small happiness from this week, a meal, a message, a moment of quiet, and notice how, just then, the wanting paused; see if you can find that pause again without the thing, and rest in the shade. When a want pulls you back into the sun, or a heavy thought about yourself arrives, ask whose it is. If you pray, you can let the resting be your prayer.
Ramana Maharshi. The teacher who said happiness isn't in things but is the self's own, and that the wise one stays in the shade.
Your line: joy is the self's own, not the thing's. Tomorrow, a different kind of teacher: Aurobindo. Day nine hundred fifty-two, the end of a week.

screen: `DAY 952 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHERE DID AUROBINDO SEE GOD?`
